newsitem.title: FRANCE: Private pensions one step from debut in France.
newsitem.headline: Private pensions one step from debut in France.

text.p: A bill to introduce private pension funds in France cleared one of the last outstanding hurdles to becoming law when it was adopted by the Senate after a second reading on Thursday.

The upper house of parliament backed the draft legislation to allow the creation of voluntary private pension funds, with the centre-right government parties securing safe passage but the opposition left-wing parties voting against the bill.

The Socialist Party vowed to repeal the future legislation if it gets into power in 1998 legislative elections and said it would try in the meantime to get it quashed by the Consitutional Council, the country's highest constitutional authority.

"Without overstating it, you are dramatically changing our system of social protection...this text is both inegalitarian for our people and dangerous for the social security regime, we will refer it to the constitutional council," Socialist Party member Marc Massion said in the Senate before the vote.

The Socialists, Communists and all the main trade unions oppose the bill, arguing that incentives for employers -- including exemptions from social security charges -- will drain money from the social security funds which finance the current state-backed retirement benefit system.
Massion said the bill would appeal "principally to the bosses of small and medium sized companies and upper level managers in big companies."
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis defended the bill against what he described as "this violent opposition."
"These fears are unfounded and based on a degree of dogmatism," he said.
The bill is scheduled go to a mixed Senate-National Assembly committee on Feburary 5 for final arbitration on the amendments, the last step before definitive adoption.

The main amendment voted by the Senate aims to reduce the amount a private pension fund can hold in any one company to five percent of the firm's share capital, from the 10 percent ceiling approved in a second reading by the National Assembly.

There was no change to the most controversial clause, already agreed between the two houses of parliament, which exempts employers from social security charges on contributions they make on behalf on employees.
Another amendment adopted by the upper house would allow employees to subscribe to a pension fund outside their company if the firm has not agreed a collective private pension deal within a year.
The bill, as agreed by both houses of parliament, will cap pension fund investment in fixed-income bonds at 65 percent in an attempt to secure investment in France's weakly capitalised stock market.

Further amendments adopted by the Senate would oblige the insurers, banks and other groups who set up pension funds to cordon them off as isolated units for prudential reasons and, to avoid conflict of interest, ensure that the pension fund voted separately at the general assemblies of firms.
